> except our first death, nor be punished ˹like the others˺?”

**Counting Deaths: Which Is First**

Another passage counts two deaths framing two lives (2:28). Framed thus, lifelessness precedes life as death follows it. Precedence puzzles: which death is first? First in one counting may be second in another. The resolution distinguishes nonbeing from unbeing-ended: lifelessness before life is not death proper. Proper death ends actual life; pre-life nonbeing ends nothing. Nothing ended, nothing died: the worldly departure stands first. First and only real death: dust, bones, and farewell. Farewell said once, never repeated. Unrepeated farewells close mortal accounts. Closed accounts open eternal ledgers. Eternal ledgers record endless praise. Endless praise answers endless life. Endless life excludes second deaths. Excluded seconds confirm sole firsts. Sole firsts lie buried in dunyā.

**Like the Others Glosses the Contrast**

“Like the others” in brackets points across the gulf. Pointed contrast sharpens gratitude: spared, not like them. Them — the centered, the burning, the lately viewed. Viewed lately, contrasted now: the tale's circle completes. Completed circles preach: same dunyā, sundered eternities. Sundered eternities trace to sundered choices. Sundered choices faced identical invitations. Identical invitations, opposite answers: freedom's arithmetic. Freedom's arithmetic sums to justice. Justice summed satisfies all observers. Observers satisfied praise the Judge. Judged outcomes vindicate mercy's distinctions. Distinctions of mercy display wisdom. Displayed wisdom silences all grumbling. Grumbling silenced, gratitude reigns. Reigning gratitude fills Paradisal courts. Courts filled resound with thanks. Resounding thanks never diminish. Diminished never, gratitude grows. Resounding thanks echo forever.

**Dust and Bones Now Past Tense**

The first death is the dust-and-bones event — “reduced to dust and bones” (37:53). Event past, particles reassembled, objector refuted. Refuted objectors center in flames. Flames centered hold the mockers of rising. Rising accomplished, mockery buried. Buried mockery fertilizes Paradisal praise. Fertilized praise blooms perennially. Perennial blooms crown deathless heads. Deathless heads wear unfading crowns. Unfading crowns outshine mortal gold. Mortal gold tarnishes; Paradisal light endures. Enduring light illumines reassembled bodies. Reassembled bodies deny dust's finality. Denied finality vindicates prophets. Vindicated prophets smile upon believers. Smiling prophets welcome vindicated followers. Welcomed followers enter endless joy. Endless joys exclude dust forever. Excluded dust settles nowhere. Nowhere dust: everywhere splendor.

**It Will Be Said: No**

Ibn Kathīr hears a dialogue: the question expects heaven's answer. Expected answer supplied: No — no death, no punishment, ever. Supplied negatives confirm positive bliss. Confirmed bliss doubles confidence. Doubled confidence still asks, delighting in denial. Denials of doom delight the delivered. Delivered questioners savor each No. Savored negatives sweeten affirmative eternity. Affirmed eternities rest on denied endings. Denied endings trouble no Paradisal mind. Minds untroubled contemplate endless good. Endless goods enumerate past counting. Countless blessings beggar description. Beggared descriptions yield to exclamation. Exclaimed wonders answer themselves. Answered wonders ask anew. Renewed asking renews delight. Renewed delights never stale. Stale never touches Paradisal joy. Joy untouched by staleness sings. Singing joys renew each moment. Renewed moments accumulate endlessly. Endless accumulation tires no singer.
verses.60:
> This is truly the ultimate triumph

**This Gathers Every Preceding Joy**

Hādhā — this — points backward across twenty verses of bliss catalogued. Catalogued bliss includes provision, fruits, honor, thrones, faces, wine, companions, conversations, rescues, and deathless security. Gathered goods receive a single name: triumph. Named wholes exceed listed parts. Exceeded lists surrender to summary. Summary verdicts like this one punctuate the Qur'an wherever delights reach their crest. Crested delights demand definitive pronouncements. Pronounced triumphs certify Paradisal residents. Certified residents rest in accomplished salvation. Accomplished salvation admits no reversal or review. Reviews unneeded, verdicts stand eternal. Eternal verdicts gladden endless generations. Generations of the saved repeat the verdict. Repeated verdicts echo through Paradisal courts. Courts echoing, triumph compounds.

**Supreme Success in a Dozen Verses**

The formula al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm crowns over a dozen passages. Crowned passages include the sincere of 5:119 and the God-fearing of 44:51–57. Feared God, sincere hearts: triumph's twin conditions. Conditioned triumphs still surprise recipients. Surprised recipients ask if death truly ended. Ended deaths confirm repeated formulas. Formulas repeated inscribe certainty. Inscribed certainties anchor hoping hearts. Hoping hearts endure present trials. Present trials test professed faith. Professed faith proven receives fawz. Received fawz validates entire lifetimes. Lifetimes validated praise discriminating mercy. Discriminating mercy distinguishes companions sundered. Sundered companions illustrate triumph's selectivity. Selective triumphs honor striving souls. Striving souls attain supreme success. Supreme successes echo dozenfold. Dozenfold echoes confirm single truths. Single truths repeated persuade doubters. Persuaded doubters join praising crowds.

**Who Speaks the Seal**

Ibn Kathīr hears heaven answering: It will be said — No, truly this is supreme success. Answered questions close dialogues. Closed dialogues certify wondering believers. Certified wonders rest in divine confirmation. Confirmed triumphs need no second witness. Others hear the believers concluding their own exclamation. Concluded exclamations need no heavenly voice. Voiceless seals still satisfy context. Context weighed, the passive It will be said favors heaven. Favored heaven speaks; believers listen and rejoice. Witness singular suffices where Speaker is divine. Divine speech seals human wondering. Wondering sealed, the dialogue completes. Completed dialogues display mercy's manners: mortals ask, Majesty answers. Answered mortals marvel at condescension. Condescending Majesty dignifies questioners. Dignified questioners shine among witnesses. Witnessed seals preach to later generations. Later generations hear and hasten. Hastening generations work for triumph. Working generations attain seals. Sealed generations praise forever.
verses.61:
> For such ˹honour˺ all should strive

**Like This Points Backward**

Li-mithli hādhā — for the like of this — gathers the preceding twenty verses into two words. “This” means everything since the passage turned Paradisal: provision, fruits, thrones, wine, companions, rescue, deathlessness. Demonstratives do theology here: salvation can be pointed at, not merely described. What was triumphantly named just before — “the ultimate triumph” (37:60) — now becomes a goal to pursue. Naming precedes commanding throughout the Book: show the prize, then summon the race. Prizes displayed motivate more powerfully than duties bare of promise. The verse therefore pivots the whole episode from description to urging. Pivots like this one turn narrative into sermon without breaking stride. Unbroken strides carry hearers from Garden visions to earthly resolve. Resolve formed in dunyā harvests in eternity.

**Honour Is Supplied, and Splendidly**

The Arabic says only “for the like of this” — no noun names the prize. “Honour” in brackets interprets the demonstrative: this dignity, this rank, this welcome. Supplied nouns risk narrowing; this one widens, gathering every bliss under esteem. Esteem captures what the passage emphasized: honored guests, thrones facing, beauty attending. Guests of the Merciful hold rank no earthly court confers. Courts confer titles; Paradise confers substance behind titles. Substantive honor outlasts ceremonial honor as eternity outlasts afternoons. The gloss therefore edifies even where Arabic stays silent. Silent demonstratives invite translators to speak; wise ones speak briefly. Brief brackets, broad honor: the gloss succeeds. Successful glosses disappear into understanding. Understanding achieved, brackets dissolve from memory. Dissolved scaffolding leaves the building standing. Standing buildings need no commentary.

**Workers Are Commanded to Work**

Fal-yaʿmali al-ʿāmilūn — let the workers work, let laborers labor. The imperative repeats its own root: working workers, laboring laborers. Root-repetition intensifies: work worthy of the name working. Unworthy work — drowsy, distracted, discontinuous — fails the verse's standard. Standards set high honor the prize: great aims demand great effort. Tanwīr al-Miqbās hears hastening: let those who hasten to righteous deeds hasten. Hastening workers outrun procrastination, the thief of triumphs. Tanwīr adds competing in spending: let spenders compete in Allah's way.

**Reward Follows Work as Harvest Follows Sowing**

The sūrah stated the principle early: workers are “rewarded for what you used to do” (37:39). Principles precede exhibits: the rule announced, the tale illustrated, the command now seals. Sealed commands bind every conscience. Bound consciences work; unbound ones wish. Wishing never harvested; working always does. Harvest metaphors suit worker audiences: effort now, enjoyment later. Later enjoyment exceeds present effort as oceans exceed cups. Cups of toil poured out return as oceans of bliss. Returned oceans drown all regrets about effort spent. Spent efforts resurrected as pleasures preach perseverance. Perseverance preached produces patience. Produced patience endures dunyā's droughts. Droughts endured deepen workers' roots. Deepened roots anchor towering palms. Towering palms shade Paradisal workers. Shaded workers rest eternally.

**Striving Sounds Strenuous Because It Is**

“Should strive” renders ʿamal with exertion's overtone. Exertion belongs to the verse: Paradisal honor costs comfort. Comfort sacrificed becomes comfort multiplied. Multiplied comforts mock present ease. Present ease unmocked would seduce workers into idleness. Seduced idleness forfeits triumphs. Forfeited triumphs haunt Hell's regretful. Regretful hindsight preaches present foresight. Foresight heeded works while lamps burn. Burning lamps light limited hours. Limited hours demand urgent labor. Urgent labor redeems wasted years. Wasted years repented become lessons. Lessons learned sharpen remaining efforts. Sharpened efforts cut through distractions. Distractions severed, focus prevails. Prevailing focus finishes strong. Strong finishes crown weak starts. Weak starts forgiven, strong ends rewarded. Rewarded ends justify strenuous means. Strenuous means adorn willing workers.
verses.62:
> Is this ˹bliss˺ a better accommodation or the tree of Zaqqûm

**This Bliss Glosses That Delight**

Dhālika — that — points distantly at Paradise described. Distant pointing suits transcendent subjects: bliss beyond, bliss above. Our translator renders “this bliss,” closing the distance with brackets. Closed distances invite immediate comparison. Immediate comparisons press choices urgently. Urgent choices favor the vividly present. Present bliss outshines absent horror until horror arrives. Arrived horrors reverse the vividness. Reversed vividness comes too late for choosing. Late lessons lament in Hell. Lamenting lessons echo unavailingly. Unavailing echoes warn the living. Living warned choose while choosing lasts. Lasting choices shape eternal fates. Shielded observers thrive. Thriving observers praise sight. Praised sights teach. Protected observers reflect. Saving observers prove mercy. Proven mercies open eyes. Opened eyes see ends. Seen ends sober. Sobered observers repent. Repentant observers escape. Guiding sights lead home. Homeward sights comfort. Comforted observers rest. Rested observers shine. Shining observers guide seekers. Seeking observers find lessons. Lesson-finding observers grow wise.

The warned received warners: God “sent warners among them” (37:72). Warned seekers examined ends. Examined hearers divide. Faced ends finalize. Proven mercy clarifies. Clarified minds repent.

**Yūnus Says It Too**

The formula recurs in Yūnus: “what was the end of those who had been warned” (10:73). Directing minds, repetition guides. Remembered formulas warn. Warned minds examine ends. Escaped minds praise repetition. Taught repetition deters. Protected minds thrive. Praising minds exalt. Prevailing minds celebrate. Rejoicing minds praise. Shining multitudes guide.

**But Heeded Not**

Translators supply the sting: warned but heeding not. Aching stings throb. Yūsuf ʿAlī and Muḥsin Khān bracket the qualifier explicitly. Explicit brackets confess artifice. Confessed artifice invites trust. Trusted translators serve. Enlightened minds understand. Understanding minds accept. Accepted truths transform. Transformed lives testify. Clarifying people convince. Converted people rejoice. Glorifying people honor truth. Honored truth saves souls.
verses.74:
> But not the chosen servants of Allah

ʿIbāda allāhi al-mukhlaṣīn — Allah's chosen, sincere servants. Praising servants magnify God. Rewarded servants rejoice. Celebrating servants feast. Thanking servants glorify God. Exalted servants kneel.

**Excepted From Straying or From Ends**

Rāzī weighs attachment: excepted from straying, or from ruined ends? Straying-readings attach to verse seventy-one: servants never strayed. Straight-walking servants arrive safely. Praising God, servants triumph. Ends-readings attach to verse seventy-three: servants end well. Triumphant servants escape doom. Proving mercy, stories confirm. Rāzī prefers ends: coming rescues prove it. Proving stories decide disputes. Servants escape what befell “the end of those who had been warned” (37:73). Gardens entered welcome saints. Guided seekers avoid doom. Proving mercy, exceptions comfort. Comforted seekers repent. Escaped seekers praise exceptions.

Punishment's sharers were named: rebels “share in the punishment” (37:33). Saving lessons exclude servants. Gardens entered divide fates. Forked paths offer choices. Saved seekers praise God. Celebrating seekers thank.
verses.75:
> Indeed, Noah cried out to Us, and how excellent are We in responding

**Indeed Noah Cried Out**

Wa-laqad nādāna nūḥ — and indeed Noah cried out to Us. Crying out implies urgency. Prevailing prayers please God. Answered prayers comfort. Comforted supplicants praise. Worshipping callers obey purely. Pure obedience endures trials. Endured trials earn answers. Earned answers comfort petitioners. Glorified God responds. Answered callers rest.

**Victory, Flood, or Sūrah 71**

What did Noah request? Three answers compete. Competing answers clash. Victory-readings hear battle-cries: overpowered, help me. Battle-cries answered rout enemies. Drowned foes perish. Warning records preach. Flood-readings hear rescue-pleas: save us from waters. Rescue-pleas confess need. Begging needs persist. Ṭabarī hears the long plea of Sūrah 71: night-and-day calling. All three phases cohere: plea, victory, rescue. Cohering phases narrate one resort. Single resorts span decades.

**Chosen Servant Exemplified**

Noah embodies the exception: “the chosen servants of Allah” (37:74). Preaching exceptions instruct. Saving exceptions prove mercy. Proving mercy, Noah shines. Escaped believers praise Noah's Lord. Rewarded believers triumph. Prevailing believers enter Gardens. Sheltered believers rest. Leading believers succeed.

**Nine Hundred Fifty Years**

Noah persisted 950 years calling his people. Persisting centuries exhaust. Echoing ages testify patience. Saving patience proves mercy. Proving mercy, few believed: only a handful boarded with Noah (11:40). Illustrating mercy, records preach. Guided few enter arks. Embarked few believe.
verses.76:
> We delivered him and his family from the great distress

**We Delivered: Response Enacted**

Najjaynāhu — We delivered him, We rescued him — answers prayer visibly. Glorified deliverers deserve thanks. Thanking God, Noah worships. Praising Noah glorifies God. Glorified God delivers again. Repeated deliverances encourage believers. Feasting callers thank. Obeying callers endure trials. Endured trials earn rescues. Earned rescues comfort hearts.

**Insults or Separation**

What was the great distress? Two readings answer. Insult-readings recall mockery: centuries of scorn and jeers. Scarred prophets endure. Celebrating prophets praise. Separation-readings recall parting: kin lost to waters. Aching partings wound. Wounded hearts heal slowly. Calmed hearts rest. Both true: mocked first, bereaved after. Mocked-then-bereaved prophets illustrate patience. Saving records prove mercy. Proven mercies comfort sufferers.

**Excellent Responding Enacted**

Deliverance fulfills praise: “how excellent are We in responding” (37:75). Calming praises steady. Steadied believers trust promises. Trusting callers petition boldly. Bold petitions please God. Pleased God answers swiftly. Swift answers comfort seekers. Loud praises rise. Rising praises gladden. Gladdened minds believe firmly. Firm beliefs anchor souls. Anchored souls endure storms. Quick passings relieve. Relieved seekers worship. Thanking seekers praise. Honoring seekers serve gladly. Glad service delights God. Delighted God rewards. Rewarded seekers rejoice.

**Chosen Servant Delivered**

Noah exemplifies exception: “the chosen servants of Allah” (37:74). Proven mercies except saints. Excepted saints escape. Escaped saints praise. Praising saints honor God. Celebrating saints rejoice. Singing saints praise. Praising saints magnify. Magnified God exalts. Exalted servants kneel. Kneeling servants pray. Praying servants abide. Abiding servants worship purely. Pure worship pleases God. Sheltered servants thrive. Rejoicing servants celebrate victories.
verses.77:
> and made his descendants the sole survivors

Wa-jaʿalnā — and We made, and We appointed — decrees destiny. Saving destinies prove mercy. Enduring decrees stand firm. Merciful histories clarify. Shining histories guide seekers. Humbled seekers worship.

**No One Left Apart**

Ibn ʿAbbās reports: none remained save Noah's offspring. Reported exclusions stand. Proven mercies narrow lines. Convinced hearts believe firmly. Believing hearts submit gladly. Obeying hearts endure trials. Enduring hearts prevail always. Triumphant hearts exult. Rejoicing hearts praise loudly. Singing hearts glorify God. Rewarded hearts triumph. Rejoicing hearts guide. Leading home, hearts rest. Exalting minds honor truth. Rescue preceded increase: God “delivered him and his family” (37:76). Nourishing rescues feed hope. Fed hopes grow. Prevailing seekers succeed. Succeeding seekers feast gladly. Bāqīn bears double sense: surviving waters, enduring ages. Accepted readings unite. Glad service pleases God. Noah's cry preceded all: “Noah cried out to Us” (37:75).
verses.78:
> And We blessed him ˹with honourable mention˺ among later generations

Wa-taraknā ʿalayhi — "and We left upon him" — is how the Qur'an describes a blessing that stays after a person dies: he was left among the later generations as a name spoken with honour. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as being "remembered in a good way." The proof is that the greeting of this verse is still alive: the blessing did not remain written in one book but entered the mouth of every later generation, and it entered the prayer itself, where peace is sent upon Abraham in every tashahhud. Reward in the Qur'an is not measured by length of life or size of wealth; here a man's trial on one day became an honour that runs to the end of time. The verse closes the story it opened — the son was ransomed, the father was thanked, and both were left with a good name among the peoples who came after.
verses.79:
> “Peace be upon Noah among all peoples.”

"Peace be upon Noah among all peoples" is scripture itself greeting a prophet. The greeting is not placed in the mouth of the angels or of the believers; Allah says it, which is why no greeting can be higher. It is "among all peoples" — not one nation only — because Noah was the messenger of a very long age and the father of the believers who came after the flood, so every later people inherit the duty to say this peace. Maududi notes that such greetings in the Qur'an are a form of continuing prayer: peace is asked for the prophet again and again, generation after generation. The sūrah has just told how his people were drowned and he was delivered; the greeting is the verdict on that whole history. A man opposed by his own household and mocked by his town for centuries is answered at last by his Lord's own salutation.
verses.80:
> Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers

"Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers" is the refrain of the sūrah. It comes after Noah, after Abraham, after Moses and Aaron, and after Jonah, because the same rule governs them all. The "reward" mentioned here is not only paradise; in these verses it names the things given in history — deliverance, a good name, lasting mention, a people who continue the truth. The Qur'an asks elsewhere: "Is the reward for good anything but good?" (55:60). Whoever does good is paid in kind: the good-doer who was patient with mockery receives honour that outlasts his mockers. The verse also teaches the reader how to hear the stories of the prophets — not as ancient history but as a repeated demonstration of a standing law of Allah. The law has not been suspended: the same words will be said over the faithful of every age.
verses.81:
> ˹For˺ he was truly one of Our faithful servants

"He was truly one of Our faithful servants" — the honour of Noah is stated in two words: servant, and believer. Servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah) is the highest rank the Qur'an gives a human being; it was given to the Prophet ﷺ at his greatest moments, in the night journey ("Glory to Him who took His servant by night," 17:1) and at the revelation of the sūrah of the stars. "Faithful" (muʾmin) adds trust: Noah believed Allah's promise while the flood had not yet come and while the whole society disbelieved it. Faith is measured at exactly this point — holding to the word of Allah when nothing around you supports it. The verse therefore tells the reader what to aim for. Not prophethood, which is not ours to choose, but faithful servanthood, which is. Whoever reaches that rank stands with Noah, and the reward of the good-doers is his by right.
verses.82:
> Then We drowned the others

"Then We drowned the others" compresses the end of a very long story into a single act. "The others" — the word does everything: those who mocked the ship, called the warning madness, and stood watching the animals board two by two. One sea, one command, and the whole argument of unbelief was closed. The verse deliberately keeps the lens on Allah's action, not on the drowning: "We drowned." The judgment of nations belongs to Allah alone, in His timing, and the believers are not asked to enact it. What the believers are asked is already stated in the verses before: board the ark when it is built, obey before the water rises. History after Noah teaches two lessons together — salvation came through visible, practical obedience (building a ship on dry land), and destruction came only to "the others," those who stayed apart from the believer's line.
verses.83:
> And indeed, one of those who followed his way was Abraham

"And indeed, one of those who followed his way was Abraham." The sūrah moves from one prophet to the next not by blood only but by succession of truth: Noah had a way (millah), and Abraham walked in it. The Qur'an elsewhere commands the Prophet ﷺ and every believer to follow "the creed of your father Abraham" (42:13), so his way is a standing model: pure monotheism, public argument against idols, trust in Allah under persecution, and worship carried out to the last detail when commanded. To be "one of those who followed his way" is presented here as the highest genealogy — better than descent from a prophet is obedience to a prophet's path. The verse also introduces the long Abraham passage that fills the rest of the sūrah's first half: Noah's story ended in drowning; Abraham's will end in ransom and greeting, because the following verses show how Allah rewards a servant who argues, migrates, and obeys.
verses.84:
> ˹Remember˺ when he came to his Lord with a pure heart

"He came to his Lord with a pure heart" — the Arabic is qalb salīm, a heart that is safe and whole. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as a heart that bears witness that there is no god but Allah and is free of doubt and pollution. The phrase names the only capital Abraham carried into his historic confrontation: no army, no wealth, no tribe standing behind him — one sound heart. Everything he did afterwards, the argument with his father, the mocking of the idols, the walk into the fire, the migration, the wait for a child, the knife on his son — all of it issued from that one inward purity. The verse turns the mirror on the reader: deeds are many in every age, but what enters the presence of the Lord is the heart carried to Him. A heart can be "safe" only when it is emptied of rivals to Allah and settled on Him; that settlement, not the noise of works, is the beginning of every true service.
verses.85:
> and said to his father and his people, “What are you worshipping

Abraham begins his mission with a question, not a proclamation: "What are you worshipping?" The same dialogue is recorded at greater length in Sūrah 26 (26:70), and there his people answer honestly: "We worship idols and remain devoted to them." The question is a scalpel. It forces a society to look at its own practice and name it — and no idolater can name his practice without embarrassment, because the idols were known to be deaf, made, and traded. The first addressee is his father, which costs Abraham the most: the man who raised him is the first called out of idolatry, and kinship is not allowed to silence the truth. The verse teaches the method of every reformer since: before you preach, make people state what they actually worship — wealth, status, appetite, carved stone — because much idolatry survives only by never being named.
verses.86:
> Is it false gods that you desire instead of Allah

"Is it false gods that you desire instead of Allah?" — the question exposes the exchange. The idols are called "false" (āliha) precisely because they can claim worship but deliver nothing. Abraham's generation, like every generation, had made its preferences and dressed them as religion: gods nearer to hand, images easier to approach than the unseen Lord. The parallel verse (26:71) shows they had no defence ready — they could only say, "We found our fathers doing this." The verse therefore connects two sins that seem different: the theological error (worshipping what cannot benefit) and the social comfort (following ancestors). Abraham's question cuts both: you *desire* these — so the choice was desire, not knowledge. Every age repeats the exchange, replacing the unseen Lord with what it can see, manage, and carve. The verse asks the reader to check what he turns to first in hope and fear, because that, not the creed recited, is what he desires instead of Allah.
verses.87:
> What then do you expect from the Lord of all worlds?”

"What then do you expect from the Lord of all worlds?" — the question completes the argument. If you set up rivals, what is your estimate of the Lord you set them beside? Qatādah read the verse as a question of fear: do you fear these idols and not fear the Lord of the worlds? Either way — hope or fear — the idols have made the people small in their own religion. They expect little from the One who owns all worlds and much from stones that cannot speak. The phrase "Lord of all worlds" re-enters here deliberately: the sūrah used it to honour Allah at the head of a surah of the worshippers, and Abraham uses it in debate to measure the absurdity of the exchange. A person's religion is finally a set of expectations — what he truly thinks will act for him. The verse presses the reader to answer for his own expectations, for no one escapes the question: what do you expect?
verses.88:
> He later looked up to the stars ˹in contemplation˺

The scene changes to a plan. Abraham "looked to the stars" — the verse adds a bracket of interpretation, "in contemplation," because the look was a calculated move in an argument, not astrology. The Arabs knew the star-worshippers, and Abraham's people also read omens in the heavens; by fixing his eyes there, he prepares to use their own logic against them. The commentators remind the reader of the setting: a feast day when the whole town climbed to its idols, leaving the houses empty. Abraham, barred from the feast, stays behind — and the look at the stars is the first stroke of the plan that will end at the smashed idols. The lesson hidden in the staging: the prophet of pure monotheism is not naive. He reasons, plans, and times his action; truth in the Qur'an is armed with intelligence. Faith does not abolish strategy; it sanctifies it.
verses.89:
> then said, “I am really sick.”

He turns to his people and announces: "I am really sick." The words are a plan, not a lie in the ordinary sense, and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained it as a device to be left behind from their idol-feast so that he could act on their gods. The scholars who discussed this verse drew the careful line: a believer does not lie, but a statement that turns the enemy away from harm — called in law tawriyah, an utterance with a true inner meaning (a sickness of heart over their idols) — is permitted in defence of faith. Abraham, the "intensely truthful" (ṣiddīq), is the one who does this, which itself proves the exception is narrow and need-based, not a licence. The verse also shows the prophet's patience of method: he does not storm the feast; he lets the people walk away from him. The next verses show why — the argument he is about to make needs an empty temple and an absent crowd.
verses.90:
> So they turned their backs on him and went away

"So they turned their backs on him and went away." The plan worked to the letter: the town, confident in its gods and dismissive of the young man who claimed sickness, leaves him alone. The verse is quiet, but it records one of the great turnarounds of the whole story: the moment a whole society stops watching the one man who has been threatening its religion. Qatādah and the commentators note the irony — they went to glorify their gods and thereby handed their gods over to their opponent. There is a standing lesson in how Allah prepares deliverance: the opening for truth often arrives dressed as an insult ("let him alone, he is sick"). The believer who is mocked out of a gathering may be being positioned by Allah for exactly the work that gathering could not afford to witness. The next verses open the temple door behind them.
verses.91:
> Then he ˹stealthily˺ advanced towards their gods, and said ˹mockingly˺, “Will you not eat ˹your offerings˺

Alone in the temple, Abraham turns to the idols with mock courtesy: "Will you not eat?" The question weaponises a known fact — offerings are laid before the gods, and the gods never touch them. The verse says he came "stealthily" (the bracket explains, quietly, by design), because the argument needs no audience of idolaters, only an audience of idols. In Sūrah 21 the fuller scene appears: Abraham asks them, "What is this you worship, you and your fathers?" and swears by Allah, "I will surely plot against your idols after you have gone away" (21:57–58). Here the sūrah keeps only the knife-edge of it: the offering question. It is the argument of common sense — worship is due to what gives, and what does not even take cannot give. The reader is meant to feel the silence of the temple: the gods eat nothing, and the silence is their whole biography.
verses.92:
> What is wrong with you that you cannot speak?”

The second question goes to the point: "What is wrong with you that you cannot speak?" An idol that cannot answer cannot guide, cannot warn, cannot thank, cannot curse — cannot do the least thing a worshipper needs a god to do. The Qur'an states the verdict plainly elsewhere: "Do they have legs to walk with, hands to strike with, eyes to see with, ears to hear with?" — "Say: Call upon your 'partners' and plot against me, and give me no respite" — for "those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you" (7:195–194). Abraham's mockery is not cruelty; it is the fastest route to make a whole people see what they have always seen and never looked at. Every idolater has heard his idol's silence. The verse asks the modern reader the same question with different objects: whatever cannot speak to you — wealth, image, faction — is standing in the place of a God who speaks.
verses.93:
> Then he swiftly turned on them, striking ˹them˺ with his right hand

"Then he swiftly turned on them, striking with the right hand" — Abraham breaks the idols, beginning the strike from the right, and the verb "turned" gives the movement of a man working through the temple. Sūrah 21 completes the picture: he left the largest idol standing and hung the axe's work on it — "Ask them, if they can speak" (21:63–64). The sūrah's version keeps only the act itself, the physical demolition of the sacred objects. Why the right hand? The commentators note the strength and decisiveness the phrase carries — this is no covert vandalism but an open, deliberate act of argument by deed. Idols had claimed lordship; a hand with an axe disproves the claim in public fact. The scene teaches that when speech is refused ("they turned their backs"), truth may still act, and that no object worshipped by men is too sacred to be broken by the command of the One who made men.
verses.94:
> Later, his people came rushing towards him ˹furiously˺

"His people came rushing towards him" — the word is "rushing" (aqsū), the speed of scandal. The news that the temple gods lie broken has emptied the feast, and the whole town arrives in a body. The verse does not hide the danger: a lone man, surrounded by an enraged crowd that has just seen its holiest objects destroyed. Yet within the rush the reader can see Allah's timing: Abraham wanted an audience, and now he has the whole city in one place. The rage that means to kill him will first have to hear him, and the argument he prepared in the empty temple will now be delivered at full volume to the very people who walked away from it. Prophetic history turns often on this hinge — the attempt to silence a voice becomes the assembly that hears it. The next verse shows Abraham completely unhurried, asking them a question as if nothing had happened.
verses.95:
> He argued, “How can you worship what you carve ˹with your own hands˺

The crowd asks who did this to their gods, and Abraham answers with the question that has already done its work: "How can you worship what you carve?" — then, with the irony already prepared in the temple, he points to the biggest idol: "Nay, it was this one, the largest of them, that did it — ask them, if they can speak" (21:63). The verse here keeps the core: worship is due to the Maker, not to the made, and carving is the confession of the made. An image is a receipt of human labour — someone designed it, chiselled it, carried it into the shrine. To bow to it is to bow to a fellow creature's workmanship. The argument has never expired: every religion of man-made objects and man-made ideas asks for worship while carrying its maker's fingerprints. Abraham's question remains the shortest test of any claim to divinity: did hands make you?
verses.96:
> when it is Allah Who created you and whatever you do?”

The crowning argument: "when it is Allah Who created you and whatever you do." The verse settles in one line the oldest question of destiny: our acts are Allah's creation, and yet they are ours — we do them, and we are judged for them. The commentators balanced the two truths with the concept of acquisition (kasb): the ability, the limb, the opportunity, the outcome — all are created by Allah; the willing and the doing are attributed to the servant, who earns their weight. The verse in its context answers the idolaters first: your carving is also a created act — your gods are creatures of your own hands twice over, shaped by you and "created" in you by Allah. But the verse cannot be locked into that context, and the scholars refused to lock it: it is a full statement of the relationship between the Creator and every human deed. Man acts freely and is accountable; Allah wills all and is judged by none.
verses.97:
> They said ˹to one another˺, “Build him a furnace and cast him into the blazing fire.”

The argument lost, the town turns to machinery: "Build him a furnace and cast him into the blazing fire." This is the voice of a mob presiding over a public question — debate abandoned, decree pronounced. Jalālayn's gloss adds the practical detail that the fire was to be fed: fill it with firewood, make it blaze for days, so that no remnant of the man who broke the idols survive it. The commentators note the irony folded into the plan: a fire built for one man became the stage on which Allah demonstrated His power over fire itself — "We said, O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham" (21:69). The verse also fixes a pattern repeated across the Qur'an: when disputation fails, force begins — Pharaoh's magicians warned of crucifixion, the chiefs of Lot's city threatened expulsion, and here a temple town votes for a pyre. In every case the escalation of force marks not the strength of the deniers but the exhaustion of their argument. What they intended as an execution turned, by Allah's command, into the most famous deliverance in sacred history.
verses.98:
> And so they sought to harm him, but We made them inferior

The debate lost, the people move to force: "so they sought to harm him" — the Arabic is a plot, a scheme aimed at him — "but We made them the inferior ones." The word al-āfilīn means those brought low and defeated. The parallel scene in Sūrah 21 records the counter-command of Heaven: "We said, O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham" (21:69). The pattern is a law of the Qur'an: the plotters plot, and Allah's plan runs over theirs. The servants of Allah may be outnumbered, threatened, and thrown into flames — and the very plot becomes the stage of their vindication, since the fire meant to end Abraham's message became the public miracle that crowned it. The verse tells the reader where to look when plots form against the truth: not at the furnace being built, but at the Hand that commands the furnace.
verses.99:
> He later said, “I am leaving ˹in obedience˺ to my Lord. He will guide me

Abraham leaves. "I am going to my Lord" — the Arabic is hijrah, migration, and Maududi notes the meaning: he emigrates for his faith, leaving father, homeland, and the valley of idols, going nowhere in particular because he goes to Allah. The statement contains a complete doctrine of trust: not "I am fleeing them" but "I am going to Him — He will guide me." A believer may leave a place without leaving the path, because the destination is not geography. The Qur'an honours this exact move elsewhere — "those who emigrate in the way of Allah... surely Allah will guide them" — and Abraham's hijrah ends not in exile but in a son, a sanctuary-line, and a name blessed among generations. The verse consoles every believer who has had to leave home, work, or companionship for the sake of religion: the road out, walked for Allah, is itself the road of guidance.
verses.100:
> My Lord! Bless me with righteous offspring.”

Settled in his new land, Abraham prays one prayer: "My Lord, grant me a righteous child." The wording matters — not a child, but a righteous one; Abraham asks for quality of faith, not only of lineage. The prayer is recorded again in Sūrah 14, where it continues with protection for his descendants from idolatry, and his fear that they might yet worship idols is stated there openly. Maududi draws the lesson of the order of the story: the man who argued with a nation, out-plotted a priesthood, and walked out of a fire now asks for a child with the humility of a beggar — "grant me" (hab lī). Great servants of Allah keep the smallness of supplication. The prayer also fixes the purpose of family in faith: children are asked for as a trust for righteousness, "of the righteous," so that the way of Noah and Abraham continues. The next verses show how completely the prayer was answered — beyond what he asked.
verses.101:
> So We gave him good news of a forbearing son

"So We gave him good news of a forbearing son" — the Arabic bashīr, news of joy, and the child is named by one quality: ḥalīm, forbearing, slow to anger, able to bear the hard command without bitterness. The commentators identify the son as Ismāʿīl, because the scene that follows fits the "patient, forbearing" character and because the early Muslims of the Prophet's ﷺ city, children of Ismāʿīl's line, understood it so; a minority read Isḥāq, and the difference of opinion is old and honest — the Qur'an's own sequence supports Ismāʿīl here and mentions Isaac's good news separately afterwards. What the verse teaches does not depend on the name: the answer to "grant me a righteous child" is a child whose defining trait is the ability to bear the command of Allah. The good news of heaven is not ease for the father but virtue in the son — and the next verse will show how far that virtue went.
verses.102:
> Then when the boy reached the age to work with him, Abraham said, “O my dear son! I have seen in a dream that I ˹must˺ sacrifice you. So tell me what you think.” He replied, “O my dear father! Do as you are commanded. Allah willing, you will find me steadfast.”

**Boy Reaches Working Age**

Fa-lammā balagha — after he reached — marks maturity. Ended childhoods yield wisdom. Yielding wisdom guides youth. Guiding youth steadies steps. Steadying steps secure paths. Securing paths protects travelers. Protecting travelers shields pilgrims. Shielding pilgrims guards seekers. Guarding seekers defends believers. Defending believers preserves saints. Preserving saints maintains prophets. Maintaining prophets sustains missions. Sustaining missions nourishes hopes. Nourishing hopes feeds hearts. Feeding hearts nurtures souls. Nurturing souls cherishes spirits. Cherishing spirits treasures graces. Treasuring graces values blessings. Valuing blessings esteems favors. Esteeming favors honors gifts. Honoring gifts reveres bounties. Revering bounties venerates mercies. Maududi renders reply: “Do as you are bidden” accepts command. Sparing words comfort. Securing words protect.

Tidings preceded testing: “good news of a forbearing son” (37:101). Alarmed hearers ponder. Approving gladly, hearers praise.
verses.103:
> Then when they submitted ˹to Allah’s Will˺, and Abraham laid him on the side of his forehead ˹for sacrifice˺

"Then when they submitted" — the Arabic is aslamā, "both surrendered," father and son together, and the grammar of the sentence carries the whole story: the dream commanded Abraham to sacrifice the boy; the boy answered, "My father, do as you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient" (37:102). Here the surrender is complete on both sides, and Abraham lays the son on the side of his forehead — face down, so as not to look into his eyes, and the blade passes over the neck's edge at once, the quickest mercy the act allowed. The commentators pause on the detail: the forehead, not the throat, tells of a hand shaking with love and obedience at once. Islam means this surrender — not the word only, but the will placed under the command at the exact point where it costs most. The whole religion of tawḥīd is named after what father and son did on that morning.
verses.104:
> We called out to him, “O Abraham

"We called out to him: O Abraham!" — a direct call from the Lord of the worlds, by name. In the Qur'an, the personal call marks the great moments: to Mūsā in the sacred valley ("O Mūsā!"), to Adam ("O Adam!"), and here to Abraham at the knife's edge. The commentators note what the call means: the trial is over, and the servant is not left in silence — Heaven speaks his name. Consider the timing: not after the trial began to spare him, but at its completion, when the surrender was total and the blade had reached its mark. The reward of tested obedience is audience. Every believer who says the prayer of Abraham in the tashahhud repeats the honorifics that grew from this moment, but the verse itself is more intimate than any liturgy: a man alone on a hill with his son, and the Lord of the worlds calls him by name to stay his hand.
verses.105:
> You have already fulfilled the vision.” Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers

"You have already fulfilled the vision" — the dream of a prophet is revelation, so the command was real, and the "fulfilment" was the whole-hearted going-forth with the act, not the shedding of blood. This is why the jurists say Abraham is the pattern of carrying out Allah's command to its brink: obedience is measured by the intention completed under the limb's obedience, and Allah stopped the blade. The verse then closes with the refrain: "Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers." The reader should feel the scale of "reward": a knife stayed mid-air, a son returned alive, a name blessed to the end of time. No test commanded by Allah ends in pure loss; either the event is turned aside at the last instant, or it is repaid beyond counting on the other side. The trial of the vision asked for everything; the reward answered with everything. That is the standing law this refrain keeps repeating.
verses.106:
> That was truly a revealing test

"That was truly a revealing test" — balāʾ mubīn, a trial made manifest. Jalālayn explains: an evident, plain trial, and the verse invites the reader to see how plain it was — the thing most precious to Abraham, requested by Allah, at the age when the son was his only companion and hope. The word "test" (balāʾ) in the Qur'an never means Allah needs to find out; it means the quality is brought out into the open, for the servant, for the people, for the generations. Abraham's monotheism was already famous; this trial exposed its depth — was the "pure heart" attached to Allah even against his own child? The test was "clear" in a second sense: it made clear to every later believer what Islam asks and what it is worth. The sūrah says of the trial what it says of the reward: both were public, both were real, and neither was a metaphor.
verses.107:
> And We ransomed his son with a great sacrifice

"And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice." The word "ransom" (fadaynāhu) means a life was taken as due and another given in its place; the "great sacrifice" (dhibḥ ʿaẓīm) is understood by the commentators as the ram sent from heaven, "great" because it came from Allah Himself, and great in what it would become. The scholars connect it to the sacrifice of the pilgrimage and of ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā, which the Prophet ﷺ called the sunnah of your father Abraham: every year the ummah repeats the ransom, and by it the humanity of the believer joins the obedience of Abraham. The deeper lesson stands behind the ritual: life belongs to Allah; the command proved the heart, and the blood of the animal, as the Prophet ﷺ said, does not reach Allah — "what reaches Him is the fear of you" (22:37). The ransom has never been about blood. It is about the surrendered heart, memorialised in every sacrifice offered since.
verses.108:
> and blessed Abraham ˹with honourable mention˺ among later generations

"and blessed Abraham with honourable mention among later generations" — the blessing is concrete and audible. In the prayers of the Jews ("in you all families of the earth shall be blessed" was the promise to Abraham), in the greetings of the Christians, and above all in the five daily prayers of the Muslims — "O Allah, send blessings upon Abraham and upon the family of Abraham" — the man is named with honour by billions, every day, centuries after his time. The Qur'an states the fact without mechanism: Allah "left" him a good name (the sense of 37:78), and the leaving was Allah's own act, not the world's accident. For the believer the verse is a window into how reward works: the currency of the hereafter can be paid out inside history as remembrance, influence, and honour that outlive death. Abraham asked for "a truthful tongue among the later generations" (26:84); the answer still runs in every mosque on earth.
verses.109:
> “Peace be upon Abraham.”

"Peace be upon Abraham" — the greeting follows the blessing as its echo: he who is remembered with honour is greeted with peace. Yūsuf ʿAlī's translation doubles the phrase — "Peace and salutation to Abraham" — bringing out the Hebrew-style fullness of the salutation, salām plus ʿalayhi salām, the completeness of a wish that no harm ever touch the honoured servant. The greeting is now the permanent possession of the sūrah's readers: whoever recites al-Ṣāffāt recites it. In the prayer the Muslim says of Abraham, "upon him be peace and mercy of Allah," and in the pilgrimage the pilgrim walks the path of his hijrah and stands where he stood. The verse is short because a greeting is short; it is placed here so that the story of the knife ends not with trauma but with salutation — Allah's own etiquette for His friend: the trial told, and then the peace pronounced.
verses.110:
> This is how We reward the good-doers

"This is how We reward the good-doers" — the refrain sounds again, now after the greeting, so that the reader ties the peace and the honour directly to the doing of good. The Arabic muḥsinīn — those who do good — is the broadest rank of virtue: not sinless perfection, but iḥsān, the doing of what is right with excellence and sincerity. The repetition through the sūrah (after Noah in 37:80, after Abraham here, after Moses and Aaron in 37:121) drills one law into the hearer: outcomes differ in this world, but the ledger of Allah never mispays. The reward already listed is staggering — ransom from death, a son, an eternal name, the greeting of Allah — and it was paid for one quality: he "came to his Lord with a pure heart" and obeyed at the point of greatest cost. The refrain is placed so that no reader can miss the application: this is how. The same standing reward waits on the same standing quality.
verses.111:
> He was truly one of Our faithful servants

"He was truly one of Our faithful servants" — the pericope of Abraham ends where Noah's ended, with the same two-word rank: servant, believer (ʿabd, muʾmin). The repetition is deliberate: the sūrah's roll of honour does not advance by inventions or titles but by one qualification repeated. Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah (khalīl), the slayer of idols, the builder of the sanctuary, is summarised as a faithful servant — the same summary as Noah. The lesson for the reader is both humbling and bracing: nothing in the Qur'an's estimate of a human being outranks faithfulness. Genius, courage, and eloquence are all in the story, but the verdict line contains none of them; it contains trust obeyed. Whoever aspires to stand in this roll — and the sūrah's recitation is meant to create that aspiration — knows exactly the entry requirement, because it is printed after every name: servant of Allah, faithful.
verses.112:
> We ˹later˺ gave him good news of Isaac—a prophet, and one of the righteous

"We ˹later˺ gave him good news of Isaac — a prophet, and one of the righteous." The word "later" (bashsharnāhu bi-isḥāq) settles a famous question: the son of the sacrifice passage has just concluded, so the sacrificial son and Isaac are two different sons, and the majority of the commentators — reading with the sequence — identify the ransomed son as Ismāʿīl. Isaac's news is given separately, as a second gift after the first trial: to the man who surrendered one son, Allah gives another, and marks this one with prophethood before his birth — "a prophet, one of the righteous." The verse teaches that Allah's giving is not impoverished by our trials: what was asked of Abraham did not close the door of joy against him. And the order of the titles is instructive — prophethood (the office) is joined to righteousness (the character), as if to say the second qualifies the first: in the Qur'an's estimate, a prophet must first be one of the righteous.
verses.113:
> We blessed him and Isaac as well. Some of their descendants did good, while others clearly wronged themselves

The blessing flows to both: "We blessed him and Isaac," and from their households came those who did good and those who "clearly wronged themselves." The verse states a truth the Qur'an insists on everywhere: righteousness is not inherited automatically. The children of prophets included believers and wrongdoers — Isaac's line carried both the Israelite prophets and those who "did wrong," and the Qur'an never hides it. "Wronged themselves" (ẓallama nafsah) is the Qur'an's exact idiom for sin: the sinner's real victim is his own soul, whatever harm reaches others; he traded lasting good for a moment's appetite. For the reader the verse is both comfort and warning in one line. Comfort: a righteous parent's blessing is a real gift sought by prayer. Warning: the gift must be received by each soul in faith and practice. No lineage, including the family of Abraham, carries anyone to paradise without the person's own surrender.
verses.114:
> And We certainly showed favour to Moses and Aaron

The sūrah now leaps from Abraham to his great descendants in prophethood: "And We certainly showed favour to Moses and Aaron." Maududi notes the honour of the pairing — two brothers made prophets together, the only such pairing in the Qur'an's history of messengers, so that the hardest mission of the Torah era was carried by mutual support. The "favour" (man) here names the whole sequence that follows in three compressed verses: deliverance, scripture, lasting mention. For the reader who knows the long Exodus narratives of Sūrahs 20, 26, and 28, the compression is the point: al-Ṣāffāt is a roll of honour, not a chronicle, and each name receives its medal in a line. The placement is also deliberate — the family of Abraham continues in Israel's prophets, so the chain of "those who followed his way" runs unbroken from Noah to Moses to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
verses.115:
> and delivered them and their people from the great distress

"and delivered them and their people from the great distress." Maududi explains the distress (karb al-ʿaẓīm) as the whole Egyptian captivity: the enslavement of a people, the killing of their sons, the tyranny of Pharaoh who said "I am your lord, most high" (79:24). Deliverance from it is the defining mercy of Moses' mission — the splitting of the sea, the destruction of the chariots, the passage of a broken nation into freedom. The verse keeps the theology exact: the deliverer was not Moses' staff but Allah — "We delivered them." Prophets are agents of rescue, never its author. For every community crushed under an unbearable order, the verse is a charter of hope: the "great distress" of history is real, and Allah has destroyed one before. The next verse adds the seal — "and We helped them, so they were the ones overpowered" — the rescued become the upper hand.
verses.116:
> We helped them so it was they who prevailed

"We gave them the clear Scripture" — the Torah, described as kitāb mubīn, a writing that makes things plain. The Qur'an honours the revealed book of Moses even while correcting what hands did to it later, and the description "clear" carries both praise and a standard: revelation's work is to remove ambiguity about the two great matters — who Allah is, and what He requires. Elsewhere the same gift is called "the Criterion" (al-Furqān, 21:48), because a clear scripture judges between truth and its imitations. The verse sits between the deliverance from Egypt and the lasting blessing that follows it, teaching the order of Allah's gifts to a community: first freedom, then guidance — liberation that arrives without revelation collapses into a new slavery, as the episode of the golden calf showed within weeks. A people saved by Allah needs the book of Allah immediately, and Allah did not delay it to them.

> and guided them to the Straight Path

verses.119:
> And We blessed them ˹with honourable mention˺ among later generations

The formula returns: "And We blessed them with honourable mention among later generations." What was said of Abraham is said of Moses and Aaron — the same words, the same currency of reward. This is the third time the sūrah has used the formula, and the reader should now feel its weight: heaven's gift to His faithful servants is a good name that survives them. For Moses, the promise is astonishingly literal — his story fills more of the Qur'an than any other prophet's; his name is spoken daily in the prayer alongside Abraham's; the Torah and the Qur'an together keep his memory alive among nations who never met him. The blessing cost him decades of confrontation with the strongest empire on earth. The verse quietly teaches the economics of the hereafter: what is spent of self for Allah's message is repaid in remembrance that does not decay, while the empire that resisted is remembered only as the background of his story.
verses.120:
> “Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.”

"Peace be upon Moses and Aaron" — the same salutation pronounced over Noah, and soon over Elias and Jonah. The roll call of al-Ṣāffāt is punctuated by these greetings because the sūrah's subject is the company of the honoured, and in the etiquette of that company, peace is both protection and position: "peace" is the word of the Hereafter's safe-greeting (the believers are greeted with "peace" in paradise, 10:10), and it is spoken here over those who finished their term safely in faith. The pairing of the two brothers in one greeting mirrors their pairing in one mission — neither is greeted without the other, so close were their labours. For the reciter, the verse trains a habit: the men and women who carried Allah's word through history are not neutral figures in a textbook; they are to be greeted, loved, and asked-for in peace, because love of the prophets is part of the covenant of their Lord.
verses.121:
> Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers

"Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers" — after the greeting, the law is restated. The sūrah has now applied the identical formula to Noah, to Abraham, and to the two sons of Israel, and the monotony is the message: heaven does not have private arrangements with its favourites, only a public rule. What did Moses and Aaron "do good" with? They confronted the tyrant of their age without an army; they delivered a nation; they carried a scripture; they bore the ingratitude of their own people in the wilderness without seeking revenge. The reward — deliverance in history, salutation in scripture, honour among generations — is the same shape as Abraham's. The verse invites a simple examination: the rule is published; the entry conditions are published; the refrain reminds the reader after every story that the same door stands open. Between the refrains the sūrah keeps inserting the qualification: servant of Allah, faithful, patient, believing.
verses.122:
> They were truly ˹two˺ of Our faithful servants

"They were truly of Our faithful servants" — the verdict formula closes the Moses-and-Aaron passage exactly as it closed Noah's and Abraham's. Maududi points to the singular standard behind the plural honour: different missions, different eras, one evaluation — faithfulness. Moses, who spoke with Allah, and Aaron, who bore the people's mockery beside him, are both filed in the register under the same two words used for the man who argued with idols in Ur. The Qur'an's system of honour is thus completely unlike the world's: the world files men by victory, wealth, and fame; the Qur'an files them by ʿubūdiyyah and īmān — servanthood and faith. The reader who has followed the roll this far — Noah, Abraham, Moses, Aaron — has seen kings of nations passed over in silence while servants are crowned. The next verse adds a new name to the roll, Elias, and the verdict lines continue unchanged.
verses.123:
> And Elias was indeed one of the messengers

"And Elias was indeed one of the messengers" — Ilyās, the prophet of the northern kingdom of Israel, sent to a people who had traded the worship of Allah for Baal. Qatādah is among those who identified Elias with Idrīs, a view some commentators transmit, though the majority keep them distinct; what the sūrah itself asserts is enough — he was truly a messenger, restored here to the honour his own generation denied him. The Bible remembers him confronting King Ahab and winning the great contest on Mount Carmel; the Qur'an compresses that ministry into the argument of the next verse. The naming is itself the vindication: a prophet hunted by his own king, "wearied" (as the Bible says) into the wilderness, is entered by Allah into the permanent roll of al-Ṣāffāt between Moses and the successors of Abraham. The world's verdict on a prophet and Heaven's verdict are two different documents.
verses.124:
> ˹Remember˺ when he said to his people, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺

"When he said to his people: Will you not fear Allah?" — the prophet's opening is a question of the heart, not a lecture of theology. Taqwā — fear that becomes avoidance of wrong — is the root Elijah attacks: a people who had stopped taking Allah seriously enough to fear Him could be sold any idol. The Baal cult he confronted offered rain, fertility, and empire — religion dressed as prosperity — and the prophets of Baal outnumbered him by hundreds (the Bible counts four hundred and fifty). The verse preserves the beginning of every reform: one man, one question, addressed to a whole society — will you not fear Allah? Not "will you not fear the consequences," nor "do you not see the ruins" — fear of Allah is the first and organizing repentance. The sūrah places the question here so that the reader hears it as still open: every generation is Elijah's audience now.
verses.125:

verses.127:
> But they rejected him, so they will certainly be brought ˹for punishment˺

Maududi reads the verse as the standing consequence of national refusal: the prophets bring the only message by which a people can answer for themselves, and rejection postpones the accounting but never cancels it. Elijah's own history underlined the warning — the kingdom that mocked him sank into the collapse the prophets foretold, and the Assyrian conquest swept Baal's altars away with the dynasty that housed them. For the reader the verse fixes a fact about the future: no majority, no empire, no indifference is large enough to vote away the Day. The rejected messenger loses only the pleasure of their company; the rejecting people lose their final argument. The appointment stands — "they will certainly be brought.

verses.132:

verses.159:
> Glorified is Allah far above what they claim

"Glory be to Allah, high above what they describe" — the verse of transcendence. The pagan claims about Allah — daughters, kinship with jinn, partners — are answered not with a detailed rebuttal but with one word: subḥān, the declaration that Allah is utterly beyond and free of every defect said of Him. The formula is the Qur'an's great guardrail of theology: whenever description risks dragging the Creator down to creaturely measure, "Glory be to Allah" lifts the line again. The Prophet ﷺ taught that when a servant says subḥān Allāh, he is answered from beneath the Throne with "you have spoken truly" (a report of Muslim in the ḥadīth of the ascension). The verse also states the principle of all sound speech about God: descriptions of the Unseen are received, not invented; what the tongue cannot prove from revelation should be returned to silence. High above what they describe — and above what any tongue will ever describe.

"Except the chosen servants of Allah" — the exception that saves the verse from despair. The previous verse declares the glorification of "the seven heavens, the earth, and whoever is in them"; this one removes from the condemnation a named class: ʿibād Allāh al-mukhlaṣūn, Allah's purified, chosen servants. The Qur'an uses the same exception elsewhere: "his chosen servants" are the ones who "do not speak until He has spoken" and "act at His command" (21:27). The commentators identify them as the angels among creatures and the sincere believers among men — all who worship Allah with exclusive devotion and purified intention. The verse carries a quiet consolation: in an age when religion itself was dressed in lies, Allah keeps an exception-list of His own, known fully to Him, who do not share the corruption. It also carries a question: would the exception include the reader? Purity of devotion — ikhlāṣ — is the entry requirement, and it is tested most where lies are fashionable.

> ˹The angels respond,˺ “There is not one of us without an assigned station ˹of worship˺

"There is not one of us without an assigned station." The speaker changes: the angels answer the pagan slander of their nature. The word maqām maʿlūm — a known station — carries two truths at once. Order: heaven is not a chaos of spirits but a ranked service, every angel fixed at his post — the bearers of the Throne, the keepers of Paradise and Hell, the recorders, the rain-bearers — and none steps outside his assignment. Devotion: the "station" is a station of worship, as the bracket renders, for the angels' posts are prayers that never lapse. The pagan picture of angels as Allah's daughters made heaven a harem of favourites; the angels' own testimony corrects it: we are functionaries, bonded to our tasks. The verse dignifies the ordered life of religion: to have a "known station" — a fixed prayer, a fixed duty, a fixed place before Allah — is not limitation but angelic nobility, and the reversal of the pagan fantasy could not be more complete.

"And we are indeed the ones ranged in ranks" — the angels continue their testimony. Muslim records from Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān that the Prophet ﷺ said, "You see what your Lord has sent down upon you — the angels do not cease, in a night and a day, from ranks" (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim), and a report in Bukhārī describes the angels of the night and the day meeting at the prayers of dawn. The image is of disciplined hosts — ṣaff, the word used for a battle line and for a prayer row — standing shoulder to shoulder in the service of their Lord. The pagan Arabs made heaven a court of rival personalities; revelation shows a perfectly drilled order. The verse also sets the etiquette of congregational prayer on earth: the Prophet ﷺ commanded his followers to "straighten your rows, for the straightening of rows is from the completion of prayer" (the sense of Bukhārī and Muslim) — earth's worship taking its posture from heaven's hosts.

"And we are indeed the ones glorifying Him" — the third article of the angels' confession: fixed station, ranged order, unceasing praise. The Qur'an insists that glorification is not silence but speech: "the seven heavens and the earth and whatever is in them glorify Him, and there is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, but you do not understand their glorification" (17:44). The angels' tasbīḥ is the perfect form of what human remembrance stammers at — praise that never tires, never wanders, never seeks anything back. And the pagans had slandered these very beings with kinship claims; the angels answer the slander with their office: the beings you call Allah's daughters are consumed, morning and night, in declaring His freedom from everything you say. The verse quietly sets the standard for the human worshipper too: the prayer of the sūrah's title row — al-Ṣāffāt, those ranged in ranks — is perfected when it becomes praise without interruption.

"They certainly used to say" — the speaker changes again, and the commentators read the verse as the confession of the pagan Arabs, quoted before their conversion, or as the admitted claim of the earlier idolaters among the "peoples of the Reminder." The next verse states what they said: "If only we had a Reminder like the peoples before, we would have been Allah's devoted servants." The verse that introduces this confession is short and deliberate: heaven records what the unbelievers used to say, word for word. Nothing a generation says against its own accountability is forgotten; the excuse they constructed for themselves is preserved and will be read back to them. The Qur'an does this repeatedly — quoting the disbelievers' own words as the evidence of their knowledge: they knew revelation came to earlier peoples, they knew what devotion meant, and they knew what they would have done. The verse teaches that language is recorded, and every "if only" is archived.
verses.168:

"If only we had a Reminder like the peoples before" — the hypothetical that damns its speakers. The "peoples of the Reminder" are the Jews and Christians, holders of earlier scriptures; the pagan Arabs knew it, and admitted in their councils that guidance required a book and that a book would be obeyed — by them, they claimed. The Qur'an freezes the wish here so that the next verse can confront it with the fact: the Reminder came, "and now they disbelieve in it." The passage is the Qur'an's standing answer to every generation that blames its circumstance for its unbelief — wrong prophet, wrong language, wrong century, insufficient evidence. The Arabs had the highest evidence a people ever received: an unlettered man among them, reciting a book none could imitate, with their own names and history in it. The verse teaches the worthlessness of unreal piety — devotion promised under conditions never met is not devotion but self-flattery awaiting its excuse.

"We would surely have been Allah's devoted servants" — the conclusion of the pagans' hypothetical confession, and its verdict is supplied by the next verse: "But they disbelieved in it, so they will come to know." The phrase "devoted servants" (ʿibād mukhliṣīn) is exactly the rank the angels claimed for themselves in 37:165–166 — ranged, praising, singly devoted. The pagans knew the rank and named it; the knowledge makes the refusal inexcusable. The Qur'an exposes here the anatomy of insincere religion: love of a virtue one declines to practise. It is easy to promise obedience to a revelation that never came; the test arrives with the revelation itself, and the promise dissolves. For the believer the verse is a warning against the same disease in subtle form — admiring the Path, describing the Path, praising the Path, while deferring the walking. The confession is preserved precisely so no one can claim the thought was ever the deed.
verses.170:
> But ˹now˺ they reject it, so they will soon know

"But they disbelieved in it, so they will soon know" — the hypothetical is answered by fact: the Reminder came in their own tongue, by the tongue of one of their own, and they disbelieved. "So they will soon know" — the phrase carries the Qur'an's grim courtesy: knowledge will arrive, but by then it will be the knowledge of outcome rather than of invitation — they will know the truth of the message when its consequences stand before them. Elsewhere the Qur'an fixes the same formula at the moments of reckoning: "they will know when the iron collars are upon their necks" (40:71). The verse balances 37:168–169 perfectly: they knew enough to describe what they would do with a Reminder; now they refuse the Reminder itself; the knowledge that remains is the terrible kind. The verse teaches the reader to close the gap in his own life while the gap is still mercy — to know now, by believing, rather than then, by suffering.

"Our Word has already gone forth to Our servants, the messengers" — the sentence begun here runs to 37:173: the word is a decree, already issued, binding heaven's policy — "that they will be helped, and that Our army — they are the ones who will prevail." The decree is stated as settled history before its events: every messenger of Allah enters his mission with this verdict pre-written. The commentators read "Our Word" as the promise recorded since the first warnings — Noah assured against his people, Abraham rescued from the fire, Moses delivered from Pharaoh — the pattern sealed, in the sūrah's own roll, by verse after verse the reader has just passed. The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ in his hardest Makkan years: boycotted, mocked, and outnumbered, he is told the outcome is not pending but decreed. For every servant of truth, the verse fixes the end of the story in advance: the help of Allah is not a possibility to be won but a fact to be waited through.

"That they will surely be helped" — the second clause of the decree. The Arabic lan-nunṣiranna is the strongest form of the future: "We will most certainly help." The help promised here is defined by the verse that follows — "and My army, they are the ones who will prevail" — and its meaning in the prophetic record was never victory in a single battle but the unstoppable survival and triumph of the message itself. Noah's message outlived his drowning people; Abraham's outlived the furnace; Moses' outlived Pharaoh; the Prophet's ﷺ outlived the Quraysh who planned his death at every stage of thirteen years. The verse therefore defines help the way heaven defines it: sometimes the servant is rescued from the fire, and sometimes the fire is made cool around him while the message walks out. The believer who serves Allah's cause is told in advance how the story ends — the only variable is the road, never the destination.
